\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a German conversation politely, choose a farewell that fits the situation, and write German's three distinctive marks — the eszett, the umlaut, and a capital on every noun.}

German parts formally with a promise to see each other again, casually with a word that travelled from French through Walloon and Low German before it got here, and softly with bis — \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{} — plus a word for time. This chapter takes auf Wiedersehen apart into the three words it is made of, then teaches bis as a recipe and fills its slot three times: bald, später, morgen. GE-C04-practice closes the arc with the first conversation that runs from hello to goodbye.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sehen]{sehen — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} and it is English \emph{see}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-sehen}



\begin{quote}
The German goodbye is a promise to \emph{see} each other again. Before you can say it, you need the verb — and you have met its spelling trick already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sehen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sehen} — \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{-en} on the end is the infinitive ending you know from \emph{gehen} and \emph{heißen}: the dictionary form of every German verb wears it.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — the same silent \emph{h} as in \emph{gehen}: it is not breathed, it only stretches the vowel. \emph{ZAY-en}.
  \item \texttt{s-voiced} — a German \textbf{s} before a vowel buzzes like English \textbf{z}. So \emph{sehen} opens with a \emph{z}, not an \emph{s}.
\end{itemize}

Put together: \emph{ZAY-en}. Compare \emph{gehen}, \emph{GAY-en} — the two verbs rhyme, and they will keep rhyming through every form.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sehen} and English \textbf{see} are the same word, both from Germanic \textbf{*sehwan}. There is no Latin in this line at all — unlike Spanish \emph{ver} and French \emph{voir}, which both come from Latin \emph{vidēre} (the \emph{vid-} you can still see in English \textbf{video} and \textbf{evident}).

So the two families split the sense of sight between them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Family} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}To see\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Still visible in English} \\
\midrule
Germanic & German \emph{sehen}, English \emph{see} & \emph{see}, \emph{sight} \\
Latin & Spanish \emph{ver}, French \emph{voir} & \emph{video}, \emph{vision}, \emph{evident} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English, as usual, ended up owning both halves.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sehen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ZAY-en}) — buzzing \emph{z}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gehen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}sehen\textquotedblright{} — they rhyme
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sehen\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} — the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sehen} mean, and which English word is it? (\textquotedblleft{}To see\textquotedblright{}; \emph{see}.) What does the \emph{h} do? (Only lengthens the vowel.) Where does Spanish \emph{ver} come from instead? (Latin \emph{vidēre} — English \emph{video}, \emph{evident}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wieder]{wieder — \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{with} that means \emph{back}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-wieder}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{sehen}, \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{} The goodbye promises to see each other \textbf{again} — so the next piece is that \textquotedblleft{}again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wieder}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wieder} — \textquotedblleft{}again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{VEE-der}: the \textbf{w} says \emph{v} and \textbf{ie} is a long \emph{ee}, both rules you already met in \emph{wie}. The final \textbf{-er} softens almost to \emph{-uh}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The obvious guess is that \emph{wieder} is English \textbf{wither}. It is not.

Its real cousin is the \textbf{with-} of \textbf{withdraw}, \textbf{withstand} and \textbf{withhold} — and that \emph{with-} is not the ordinary English \emph{with} meaning \textquotedblleft{}alongside.\textquotedblright{} It is an older word meaning \textbf{back} or \textbf{against}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to with\textbf{draw} is to draw \textbf{back}
  \item to with\textbf{stand} is to stand \textbf{against}
  \item to with\textbf{hold} is to hold \textbf{back}
\end{itemize}

That older sense is exactly what \emph{wieder} still carries: \textbf{back, again}. So when a German says \emph{wieder}, they are saying the \emph{with-} of \emph{withdraw}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wieder\textquotedblright{} (\emph{VEE-der}) — \emph{v}, then a long \emph{ee}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}withdraw\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}withstand\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{with-} that means \emph{back}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wieder sehen\textquotedblright{} — to see again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{wieder} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Again.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it hiding in? (The \emph{with-} of \emph{withdraw}.) What does that \emph{with-} mean there? (\textquotedblleft{}Back\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} — not \textquotedblleft{}alongside.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[auf]{auf — \textquotedblleft{}on, upon,\textquotedblright{} and it is English \emph{up}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-auf}



\begin{quote}
Two pieces down, one to go. The formal goodbye opens with a three-letter word that turns out to be one you say constantly in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: auf}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{auf} — \textquotedblleft{}on, upon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{au-diphthong} — German \textbf{au} is the \emph{ow} of English \emph{house}, never the \emph{aw} of \emph{caught}. So \emph{auf} rhymes with English \textbf{owf}, not with \emph{oaf}.
  \item \texttt{f-final} — the \textbf{f} is crisp and unvoiced at the end.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{auf} is English \textbf{up}. The vowel drifted — German widened it to \emph{au}, English kept it short — but it is one word, and the meanings still overlap almost exactly:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{auf} & up, upon, on \\
\emph{aufstehen} & to stand \textbf{up} \\
\emph{aufmachen} & to make \textbf{up}, to open \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English \textbf{upon} is literally \emph{up} + \emph{on}, which is the same doubling German gets from \emph{auf} alone. That is why \emph{auf} translates sometimes as \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{} and sometimes as \textquotedblleft{}on\textquotedblright{}: English split the job into two words and German never did.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}auf\textquotedblright{} (\emph{owf}) — the \emph{ow} of \emph{house}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}auf\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{} — the same word
  \item \textquotedblleft{}auf wieder sehen\textquotedblright{} — on the seeing-again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{auf} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}On, upon.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Up}.) How is \textbf{au} pronounced? (Like the \emph{ow} in \emph{house}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[auf Wiedersehen]{auf Wiedersehen — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}till we see again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-auf-wiedersehen}



\begin{quote}
Three lessons, three words. Now snap them together — nothing here is new.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: auf Wiedersehen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{auf Wiedersehen} — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} to a stranger, an elder, or on the telephone.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{owf VEE-der-zay-en}. Piece by piece:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{auf} & on, upon \\
\emph{wieder} & again \\
\emph{sehen} & to see \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So it reads \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}on the seeing-again\textquotedblright{}} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}until we see each other again.\textquotedblright{} Note the capital \textbf{W}: welded together the three words became a \emph{noun}, and German capitalises every noun. \emph{Ein Wiedersehen} on its own is \textquotedblleft{}a reunion.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{culture}
Set the three goodbyes side by side and each language shows what it thinks parting is:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{Goodbye} & \textbf{The metaphor} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{auf Wiedersehen} & \textquotedblleft{}till we \textbf{see} again\textquotedblright{} \\
French & \emph{au revoir} & \textquotedblleft{}till the \textbf{re-seeing}\textquotedblright{} \\
Spanish & \emph{adiós} & \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{God}\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

German and French shake hands on a re-seeing; Spanish commends you to God. The German and the French are not merely similar — they are the same sentence built from each language's own parts.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}auf Wiedersehen\textquotedblright{} — \emph{owf VEE-der-zay-en}
  \item pull it apart — \textquotedblleft{}auf\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wieder\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}sehen\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}auf Wiedersehen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}au revoir\textquotedblright{} — the same sentence, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{auf Wiedersehen} literally say? (\textquotedblleft{}On the seeing-again.\textquotedblright{}) What are its three pieces? (\emph{Auf}, \emph{wieder}, \emph{sehen}.) Why the capital \textbf{W}? (The welded word is a noun, and German capitalises nouns.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tschüss]{tschüss — the casual \textquotedblleft{}bye\textquotedblright{} that used to say \textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-tschuss}



\begin{quote}
Between friends, Germans almost never say the full \emph{auf Wiedersehen}. They say one clipped syllable — which hides the best secret in this chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tschüss}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{tschüss} — \textquotedblleft{}bye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{tsch-ch} — \textbf{tsch} is the \emph{ch} of English \textbf{ch}urch. So the word starts \emph{chü-}, not \emph{tsh-oo}.
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — \textbf{ü} is made the way you made \textbf{ö}, but starting from \emph{ee} instead of \emph{ay}: say \textbf{ee}, then round your lips without moving your tongue.
\end{itemize}

Together: \emph{chüss}, short and clipped, rhyming roughly with a rounded \emph{chuess}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tschüss} looks purely German. Trace it back and it leaves the country entirely:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{Form} & \textbf{Language} \\
\midrule
1 & \emph{adieu} — \textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{} & French \\
2 & \emph{adjûs} & Walloon (southern Belgium) \\
3 & \emph{atschüs} & Low German \\
4 & \emph{tschüss} & modern German \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And since French \emph{adieu} is \emph{à Dieu}, \textquotedblleft{}to God,\textquotedblright{} the breeziest German goodbye is a far-travelled cousin of French \textbf{adieu} and Spanish \textbf{adiós} — all three the same small blessing, just worn down further at each step.

The friendliest, most throwaway German goodbye is secretly the most solemn one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which goodbye, to whom}]
This is \textbf{register} — the same split you have drilled since \emph{du} and \emph{Sie}. Pick the parting to match the relationship:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Say} & \textbf{To} \\
\midrule
\emph{tschüss} & friends, family, peers, casual shops \\
\emph{auf Wiedersehen} & strangers, elders, officials, the telephone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

If you would say \emph{Sie} to them, say \emph{auf Wiedersehen}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
You will also hear \textbf{tschau}. That one is Italian \emph{ciao}, borrowed straight and respelt to German spelling rules — so German ended up with two casual goodbyes imported from two different Romance languages.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ee\textquotedblright{} then round your lips — \textquotedblleft{}ü\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tschüss\textquotedblright{} — \emph{chüss}, short and clipped
  \item the chain — \textquotedblleft{}adieu\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}adjûs\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}atschüs\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}tschüss\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{tschüss} secretly mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To God\textquotedblright{} — it is \emph{adieu}.) Which Spanish word is its cousin? (\emph{Adiós}.) Whom do you say it to? (Anyone you would call \emph{du}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bis]{bis — \textquotedblleft{}until,\textquotedblright{} and the shape of every soft goodbye}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-bis}



\begin{quote}
You have the formal goodbye and the casual one. Between them sits a whole family of softer partings, and every one of them starts with the same small word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bis}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bis} — \textquotedblleft{}until, up to.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{biss}: a short \emph{i} as in English \emph{bit}, and a crisp unvoiced \textbf{s} at the end — this one does \emph{not} buzz, because the buzzing rule only applies before a vowel.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: bis plus a time word}]
\emph{bis} is a \textbf{recipe}, not a phrase. Put a word for time after it and you have a goodbye:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{bis} + \emph{a time} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you \emph{then}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The other two languages in this book build their soft goodbyes exactly the same way, which means once you own the recipe you own three languages' worth of it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{The preposition} & \textbf{Example} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{bis} & \emph{bis …} \\
Spanish & \emph{hasta} & \emph{hasta …} \\
French & \emph{à} & \emph{à …} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The next three lessons each supply one time word to pour into the slot.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis\textquotedblright{} (\emph{biss}) — short \emph{i}, crisp \emph{s}
  \item the three prepositions — \textquotedblleft{}bis\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}hasta\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis …\textquotedblright{} and leave the slot open
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bis} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until, up to.\textquotedblright{}) What has to follow it to make a goodbye? (A word for time.) Which Spanish and French words do the same job? (\emph{Hasta} and \emph{à}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bald]{bald — \textquotedblleft{}soon,\textquotedblright{} which is English \emph{bold}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-bald}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Bis} is waiting for a time word. Here is the first one — and it is an English word you would never have guessed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bald}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bald} — \textquotedblleft{}soon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{balt}, not \emph{bald}: the final \textbf{d} hardens to \textbf{t} by \textbf{final devoicing}, the rule you met on \emph{und} and on \emph{Tag}. It has nothing to do with English \emph{bald} (hairless) — that is a pure coincidence of spelling.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bald} is English \textbf{bold}.

Old High German \emph{bald} meant \textquotedblleft{}bold, brave, quick.\textquotedblright{} Then the sense drifted along a line that is easy to walk: what is done \textbf{boldly} is done \textbf{without hesitating} $\to$ done \textbf{quickly} $\to$ happening \textbf{soon}.

German followed the speed. English followed the courage. One word, two destinations — and English still keeps a trace of the German path in the archaic \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}full boldly\textquotedblright{}} meaning \emph{promptly}, and in the way \emph{bold} can still mean \emph{sudden} in older writing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bald\textquotedblright{} (\emph{balt}, hard \emph{t})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bald\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}bold\textquotedblright{} — one word, two senses
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis bald\textquotedblright{} — until soon
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bald} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Soon.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Bold} — not \emph{bald}.) How did \textquotedblleft{}brave\textquotedblright{} become \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}? (What is done boldly is done quickly.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bis bald]{bis bald — \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-bis-bald}



\begin{quote}
The recipe and the first ingredient are both yours. Pour one into the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bis bald}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bis bald} — \textquotedblleft{}until soon\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you soon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{biss BALT}, with the stress on the second word and that final \textbf{d} hardening to \textbf{t}.

Use it when you genuinely expect to see the person before long — it carries a small promise the way English \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{} does, and it sounds odd to someone you are unlikely to meet again.

Its twins: Spanish \emph{hasta pronto}, French \emph{à bientôt}. All three are the same two-word recipe — preposition plus \textquotedblleft{}soon.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis bald\textquotedblright{} — \emph{biss BALT}
  \item the three twins — \textquotedblleft{}bis bald\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}hasta pronto\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à bientôt\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tschüss, bis bald!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bis bald} mean, word for word? (\textquotedblleft{}Until soon.\textquotedblright{}) When would you not use it? (When you do not expect to see the person before long.) What is the recipe? (\emph{Bis} plus a time word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[spät]{spät — \textquotedblleft{}late,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{später}, your first comparative}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-spaet}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Bis bald} is for soon. For a vaguer \textquotedblleft{}see you around,\textquotedblright{} German needs \textquotedblleft{}later\textquotedblright{} — and it builds that from \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{} exactly the way English does.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: spät}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{spät} — \textquotedblleft{}late.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{ä} is the vowel you met in \emph{Nächte}: roughly the \emph{e} of English \emph{bed}, held a little longer.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{st-initial-scht} — a German \textbf{st} at the \emph{start} of a word is said \textbf{sht}. So \emph{spät} opens like English \emph{shp}, not \emph{sp}: \textbf{shpayt}.
\end{itemize}

The same rule gives \emph{Stadt} as \emph{shtat} and \emph{Straße} as \emph{shtrahsse}. It is one of the fastest ways to stop sounding like a beginner, and it costs one rule.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Add \textbf{-er} and you have the comparative:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{spät} & late \\
\emph{spät\textbf{er}} & lat\textbf{er} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That \textbf{-er} is not a coincidence and not a borrowing — English and German inherited the same comparative ending from the same ancestor. \emph{Late/later}, \emph{spät/später}: one pattern, two languages.

So the second goodbye in the family is \textbf{bis später}, \textquotedblleft{}until later\textquotedblright{} — the twin of Spanish \emph{hasta luego} and French \emph{à plus tard}, and the one to reach for when you have no idea when you will actually meet again.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}spät\textquotedblright{} (\emph{shpayt}) — \emph{sht}, not \emph{st}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}spät\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}später\textquotedblright{} — late, then later
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis später\textquotedblright{} — until later
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{spät} mean, and \emph{später}? (\textquotedblleft{}Late\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}later.\textquotedblright{}) How is an initial \textbf{st} pronounced? (\emph{Sht} — \emph{shpayt}.) Which ending makes the comparative, in both languages? (\textbf{-er}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bis später]{bis später — \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-bis-spater}



\begin{quote}
Second ingredient into the same slot — and this one commits to nothing at all, which is exactly why it is the most used.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bis später}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bis später} — \textquotedblleft{}until later\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you later.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{biss SHPAY-ter} — remember the initial \textbf{st} is \emph{sht}.

Where \emph{bis bald} promises \textquotedblleft{}before long,\textquotedblright{} \emph{bis später} promises nothing: it is the German equivalent of a wave. That vagueness makes it the safe default when you have no idea when you will meet again.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{French} \\
\midrule
\emph{bis später} & \emph{hasta luego} & \emph{à plus tard} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis später\textquotedblright{} — \emph{biss SHPAY-ter}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis bald\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}bis später\textquotedblright{} — soon, then vaguely
  \item the twins — \textquotedblleft{}hasta luego\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à plus tard\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bis später} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until later.\textquotedblright{}) How does it differ from \emph{bis bald}? (\emph{Bald} promises soon; \emph{später} promises nothing.) How do you say the initial \textbf{st}? (\emph{Sht}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[morgen]{morgen — \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same word doing a second job}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-morgen-tomorrow}



\begin{quote}
No new word this time — a word you have had since chapter one, doing something you have not seen it do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: morgen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{morgen} — \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same spelling as the \emph{Morgen} of \emph{Guten Morgen}, same sound: \emph{MOR-gen}, with the German \textbf{r} made at the back of the throat.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the capital letter splits the sense}]
German capitalises every noun. That rule usually just makes text look busy — here it does real work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Written} & \textbf{Part of speech} & \textbf{Means} \\
\midrule
\emph{der} \textbf{M}orgen & noun & the morning \\
\textbf{m}orgen & adverb & tomorrow \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Guten Morgen!} is \textquotedblleft{}good \textbf{morning}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Bis morgen} is \textquotedblleft{}until \textbf{tomorrow}.\textquotedblright{} The capital is the only thing telling them apart on the page — and once you know that, German's noun-capitalisation stops being decoration and starts being punctuation you can read.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
This morning-becomes-tomorrow move is not a German quirk. All three languages make \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} out of \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{Morning} & \textbf{Tomorrow} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{Morgen} & \emph{morgen} \\
Spanish & \emph{mañana} & \emph{mañana} \\
French & \emph{matin} & \emph{demain} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And English did it too, then half forgot: \textbf{morrow} meant \emph{morning}, and \textbf{tomorrow} is literally \emph{to (the) morrow}. So \emph{bis morgen} is \textquotedblleft{}see you on the morrow,\textquotedblright{} almost word for word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Morgen\textquotedblright{} — good morning, capital M
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis morgen\textquotedblright{} — until tomorrow, small m
  \item \textquotedblleft{}morrow\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}morgen\textquotedblright{} — the same old word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two meanings of \emph{morgen}? (\textquotedblleft{}Morning\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}) What tells them apart in writing? (The capital letter — nouns take one.) Which English word is the old \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Morrow}, still inside \emph{tomorrow}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bis morgen]{bis morgen — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-bis-morgen}



\begin{quote}
Third ingredient, and the most definite of the three: a goodbye with an actual date on it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bis morgen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bis morgen} — \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{biss MOR-gen}. Small \textbf{m}: here \emph{morgen} is the adverb \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} not the noun \emph{der Morgen}, \textquotedblleft{}the morning.\textquotedblright{}

This is the one you say leaving work, or leaving a class you both attend again the next day. Unlike \emph{bis bald} and \emph{bis später}, it makes a claim that can be checked.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the bis… family, complete}]
One preposition, three time words, three goodbyes — and the same three in Spanish and French, built the same way:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{Means} & \textbf{Spanish / French twin} \\
\midrule
\emph{bis bald} & soon & \emph{hasta pronto} / \emph{à bientôt} \\
\emph{bis später} & later & \emph{hasta luego} / \emph{à plus tard} \\
\emph{bis morgen} & tomorrow & \emph{hasta mañana} / \emph{à demain} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You now hold German's whole farewell set: the formal \emph{auf Wiedersehen}, the casual \emph{tschüss}, and these three soft partings.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bis morgen\textquotedblright{} — \emph{biss MOR-gen}, small \emph{m}
  \item all three — \textquotedblleft{}bis bald\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}bis später\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}bis morgen\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tschüss, bis morgen!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bis morgen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}) Why the small \textbf{m}? (It is the adverb \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} not the noun \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}) Name all three \emph{bis…} goodbyes. (\emph{Bald}, \emph{später}, \emph{morgen}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ß]{ß — the letter that is two \emph{s}'s in a coat}

\label{lesson:GE-W01-eszett}



\begin{quote}
German has one letter no other Latin alphabet uses. You have already written it without being told what it was: \emph{heißen}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ß}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ß} — the \emph{eszett}, or \emph{scharfes S}, \textquotedblleft{}sharp S.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It is not a capital \emph{B}, and it is not exotic. It is \textbf{ss} wearing a single character, and it always sounds like a plain sharp \emph{s} — never a \emph{z}, never a \emph{b}.

It is a \textbf{ligature}: two letters fused into one shape. Its name says which two. \emph{Es-zett} is literally \textquotedblleft{}s-z\textquotedblright{} — in the old German hand the \textbf{long s} (a tall \emph{s} drawn like an \emph{f} without its crossbar) was joined to a following \emph{s} or \emph{z}, and the join hardened into \textbf{ß}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ß after long, ss after short}]
Modern spelling gives it one clean job, and it is a genuinely useful one — the letter tells you how long to hold the vowel \emph{before} it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ß — long vowel} & \textbf{ss — short vowel} \\
\midrule
\emph{Straße} (long \emph{a}) & \emph{Fluss} (short \emph{u}) \\
\emph{Fuß} (long \emph{u}) & \emph{muss} (short \emph{u}) \\
\emph{weiß} (diphthong \emph{ei}) & \emph{Kuss} (short \emph{u}) \\
\emph{groß} (long \emph{o}) & \emph{Schloss} (short \emph{o}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So seeing \textbf{ß} means \textquotedblleft{}the vowel before me is long.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Straße} stretches its \emph{a}; \emph{Fluss} clips its \emph{u}. One letter, two pieces of information.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing — drawing the eszett}
Draw it as a tall loop joined to a descending tail — the long-s curve, then the s/z finish. Copy \textbf{weiß} once with the model in view, then \textbf{Straße}.

Say each word as you finish it, and stretch the vowel the \textbf{ß} is telling you to stretch.

\begin{culture}
Two things worth knowing about where you will and will not see it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{It has no everyday capital.} No German word begins with \emph{ß}, so in ALL-CAPS you traditionally write \textbf{SS}: \emph{STRASSE}. A capital eszett was finally made official in 2017, but \emph{SS} is still what you will see.
  \item \textbf{Switzerland dropped it entirely.} Swiss German always writes \emph{ss} — \emph{Strasse}. So \emph{ß} on a sign is a Germany-and-Austria marker.
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two letters is \textbf{ß} made of, and what does its name say? (\emph{s} and \emph{z} — \emph{es-zett}.) What does it tell you about the vowel before it? (That it is long.) How is it written in all-caps, and where is it not used at all? (\emph{SS}; Switzerland.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ä ö ü]{ä ö ü — the two dots that used to be an \emph{e}}

\label{lesson:GE-W02-umlauts}



\begin{quote}
You have already made two of these sounds — the \textbf{ö} of \emph{schön} and the \textbf{ü} of \emph{tschüss}. Now meet the mark itself, and what it is doing there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the umlaut}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Umlaut} — the two dots on \textbf{ä ö ü}, which shift the vowel \emph{forward} in the mouth.
\end{quote}

\emph{Um-laut} is \textquotedblleft{}around-sound\textquotedblright{} (\emph{um}, around + \emph{Laut}, sound). Say the plain vowel, then brighten it toward \emph{ee}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Plain} & \textbf{Umlauted} & \textbf{How} \\
\midrule
a $\to$ \textbf{ä} & \emph{Mann} $\to$ \emph{Männer} & \emph{ah} becomes the \emph{e} of \emph{bed} \\
o $\to$ \textbf{ö} & \emph{schon} $\to$ \emph{schön} & \emph{oh} becomes a rounded \emph{eh} \\
u $\to$ \textbf{ü} & \emph{Mutter} $\to$ \emph{Mütter} & \emph{oo} becomes \emph{ee} with rounded lips \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They look like the French tréma and do the opposite job: a tréma \textbf{splits} two vowels, an umlaut \textbf{changes} one.

\begin{cousinweb}
The dots are a fossil. The fronting was originally caused by an \textbf{e} in the \emph{next} syllable, and scribes marked it by writing a tiny \textbf{e above the vowel}. In the old German hand that \emph{e} was two little vertical strokes — which, shrunk and simplified, became two dots.

So an umlaut is a \textbf{flattened \emph{e} sitting on top of the vowel}, and that is exactly why the ASCII fallbacks put it back on the line:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{With dots} & \textbf{Ghost \emph{e} restored} \\
\midrule
\emph{Müller} & Mueller \\
\emph{schön} & schoen \\
\emph{Bär} & Baer \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the umlaut does real work}]
Umlauts are not decoration. Fronting a vowel is how German marks whole grammatical changes, so learn to \emph{expect} it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Base} & \textbf{Umlauted} & \textbf{What changed} \\
\midrule
\emph{Mann} (man) & \emph{Männer} & plural \\
\emph{Buch} (book) & \emph{Bücher} & plural \\
\emph{groß} (big) & \emph{größer} & comparative \\
\emph{Hund} (dog) & \emph{Hündchen} & diminutive \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

When a German word brightens its vowel, something grammatical happened to it — usually \emph{more than one}, \emph{more}, or \emph{smaller}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing — the two dots}
Two dots, side by side, sitting squarely \textbf{above} the vowel — not slanted, and not joined. Copy \textbf{schön} once with the model in view, then \textbf{Mütter}.

Say each word as you finish it, and let the vowel brighten as you write the dots.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mann\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Männer\textquotedblright{} — hear the vowel brighten for the plural
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mutter\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Mütter\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ee} with rounded lips
  \item \textquotedblleft{}schön\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}schoen\textquotedblright{} — put the ghost \emph{e} back down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Umlaut} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Around-sound.\textquotedblright{}) What are the dots, historically? (A shrunken \emph{e} that migrated on top.) What is the fallback spelling for \emph{ü}? (\emph{ue}.) Name one grammar job the umlaut does. (Plural, comparative, or diminutive.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Großschreibung]{Großschreibung — why German capitalises every noun}

\label{lesson:GE-W03-capitalization}



\begin{quote}
You met this rule with \emph{der Tag}, and you used it to tell \emph{Morgen} from \emph{morgen}. Now here it is in full — and it turns out to be doing more work than it looks.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Großschreibung}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Großschreibung} — \textquotedblleft{}capital-writing.\textquotedblright{} Every noun takes a capital, anywhere in the sentence.
\end{quote}

Not just names or sentence starts — \emph{every} noun:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Der Hund} frisst \textbf{das Essen} in \textbf{der Küche}. — \textquotedblleft{}The dog eats the food in the kitchen.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three nouns, three capitals, two of them mid-sentence. Also capitalised: the polite \emph{Sie}, and any word \emph{used as} a noun (\emph{das Gute}, \textquotedblleft{}the good\textquotedblright{}).

(The word itself shows off two things you now know: the \textbf{ß}, and the initial \textbf{st} said \emph{sht} — \emph{GROHSS-shry-boong}.)

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the capital is a part-of-speech signal}]
The capital carries \textbf{meaning}. It separates words spelt alike that do different jobs:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Lower-case} & \textbf{Capital, so a noun} \\
\midrule
\emph{essen} — to eat & \emph{das Essen} — the food \\
\emph{jung} — young & \emph{der Junge} — the boy \\
\emph{laut} — loud & \emph{der Laut} — the sound \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the same machinery that split \emph{morgen} from \emph{Morgen}. With \emph{der/die/das} in front as well, German flags its nouns \textbf{twice} — which is why long German sentences are easier to parse, not harder.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English used to do this too: read a page of 1700s English and the Nouns are Capitalised. English dropped the habit in the eighteenth century; German kept it and wrote it into the rules. It is a living fossil of older European printing.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing — applying the rule}
Capitalise the first letter of every noun, wherever it sits. Two tests if you are unsure: is there a \emph{der/die/das} in front, or does it end in \emph{-ung}, \emph{-heit} or \emph{-schaft}? Those are noun factories — \emph{Zeitung}, \emph{Freiheit}, \emph{Freundschaft}.

Copy \textbf{Der Hund frisst das Essen} once, then write \emph{Guten Morgen} and \emph{bis morgen} one under the other and check every capital.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Der Hund frisst das Essen\textquotedblright{} — every noun capitalised
  \item \textquotedblleft{}essen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}das Essen\textquotedblright{} — the capital flips it from doing to thing
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Morgen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}bis morgen\textquotedblright{} — the same flip, in a word you own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which words does German capitalise? (Every noun, anywhere — plus \emph{Sie}.) What does the capital tell you? (That the word is a noun: \emph{essen} versus \emph{das Essen}.) Which language used to do this and stopped? (English, in the 1700s.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — hello to goodbye, in one conversation}

\label{lesson:GE-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. This is the first conversation you can run from the first word to the last — everything in it has had its own lesson.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which farewell, when}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{You are…} & \textbf{Say} \\
\midrule
formal, to a stranger & \emph{Auf Wiedersehen.} \\
casual, to a friend & \emph{Tschüss.} \\
meeting again soon & \emph{Bis bald.} \\
making no promises & \emph{Bis später.} \\
leaving for the day & \emph{Bis morgen.} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Everything from your first greeting to here, in one conversation:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Hallo! Ich heiße Anna. Wie heißen Sie?} & Hello! My name is Anna. What is your name? \\
\emph{Ich heiße Peter. Freut mich.} & My name is Peter. Pleased to meet you. \\
\emph{Wie geht es Ihnen?} & How are you? \\
\emph{Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?} & Well, thanks. And you? \\
\emph{Sehr gut. Bis morgen, Peter.} & Very well. See you tomorrow, Peter. \\
\emph{Bis morgen, Anna. Auf Wiedersehen!} & See you tomorrow, Anna. Goodbye! \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Between friends, that last line becomes \emph{Tschüss, bis morgen!} — and note that the whole exchange stayed formal because it opened formally with \emph{Sie}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item the closing pair — \textquotedblleft{}Bis morgen.\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}Auf Wiedersehen!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the casual version of that close — \textquotedblleft{}Tschüss, bis morgen!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es Ihnen? — Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the whole conversation without looking. Which goodbye promises a re-seeing? (\emph{Auf Wiedersehen}.) Which one is secretly \textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Tschüss}.) Which would you use leaving a class you both attend tomorrow? (\emph{Bis morgen}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
